paragraphs: Jailbreak methods can look successful while producing very different kinds of prompts and requiring different amounts of computation. This paper introduces a shared threat model to make comparisons more principled. Its central question is whether an attack resembles text that is likely to occur in the underlying text distribution.

The authors build an N-gram language model using one trillion tokens. This model evaluates short sequences of words or tokens through their observed frequency, providing an interpretable measure that does not depend on a particular large language model. They then adapt existing attacks to this common evaluation framework.

Under these comparisons, attack success against modern safety-tuned models is lower than previously reported, and discrete optimization attacks substantially outperform recent attacks driven by language models. The analysis also identifies a recurring mechanism: effective attacks exploit unusual two-token sequences, including absent combinations and rare combinations associated with sources such as Reddit or code. These findings connect attack effectiveness to identifiable textual patterns while showing how evaluation conditions affect apparent success.
icml-2025-an-interpretable-n-gram-perple.tldr: An interpretable N-gram threat model enables comparable jailbreak evaluations and reveals lower success rates and frequent exploitation of rare token pairs.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization uses a predictive model and its uncertainty to decide which input to evaluate next. This paper develops BARK, a model that connects Bayesian Additive Regression Trees with Gaussian processes. The goal is to combine the structure of tree models with uncertainty information suitable for guiding optimization.

BARK defines its kernel through agreement between trees and explores possible tree kernels using Markov chain Monte Carlo. Instead of sampling only individual functions, it samples Gaussian processes, each of which describes a distribution over functions. Those distributions support acquisition functions, which guide the choice of subsequent evaluations. The sampling also accounts for uncertainty about the tree structure itself.

The tree-based construction enables global optimization over the surrogate model, including spaces containing mixed feature types. This matters because choosing the next evaluation requires optimizing the model's guidance as well as fitting the model. Experiments on synthetic and applied benchmarks report strong performance, attributed to the combination of the fully Bayesian surrogate and its optimization procedure. The global optimization claim concerns the surrogate used to guide the search.
icml-2025-bark-a-fully-bayesian-tree-ker.tldr: BARK combines tree kernels with Gaussian processes to guide black-box optimization while accounting for uncertainty in tree structure.

paragraphs: Regularization controls how much complexity a model can use, but selecting its strength often requires extensive manual tuning. Cross-regularization makes those controls part of the training process. It uses gradients from validation data to adjust regularization parameters as the model learns, turning complexity selection into an ongoing optimization problem.

The method assigns distinct responsibilities to the two data sources: training data guides feature learning, while validation data guides complexity controls. The authors establish convergence to cross-validation optima and report that the relevant computational cost scales only with the dimension of the regularization parameters. This makes the number of adjustable controls central to the method's computational requirements.

When implemented by injecting noise into neural networks, the method reveals unexpectedly high tolerance for noise and regularization patterns that depend on the architecture. These patterns emerge during training rather than being specified individually beforehand. The framework also accommodates data augmentation and uncertainty calibration. Its practical contribution is a simple gradient-based route to adapting these choices within one training run.
icml-2025-cross-regularization-adaptive-.tldr: Cross-regularization uses validation gradients to adapt complexity controls during training, with convergence guarantees and single-run efficiency.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical account of how deep linear networks learn from random initialization. The analysis concerns large network widths and large quantities of random data. Although each layer is linear, the layered training problem provides a setting for examining how width, depth, data, and parameter scaling jointly influence gradient descent.

The theory captures the benefit of increasing width under mean-field or maximum-update parameterizations, along with effects that support transferring hyperparameters across widths. It contrasts these behaviors with neural-tangent parameterization, where optimal learning rates change with width. The authors analyze both residual and non-residual networks. For residual networks, scaling branches by the inverse square root of depth enables an infinite-depth limit.

The work also compares one-pass stochastic gradient descent with training that repeatedly uses the same data. Finally, the model reproduces accelerated power-law learning dynamics for data with power-law structure in the rich regime. Together, these results organize several scaling phenomena within one analytical framework, with the conclusions grounded in the stated deep-linear, large-width, random-data setting.
icml-2025-deep-linear-network-training-d.tldr: A theory of deep linear networks connects training dynamics to width, depth, data reuse, and hyperparameter transfer.

paragraphs: DEFAME is a modular pipeline for checking open-domain claims containing text and images. It uses multimodal language models in a zero-shot setting and gathers evidence as part of verification. The system treats images as relevant both within the claim being checked and within the material used to assess it.

Its six-stage process dynamically chooses tools and determines how deeply to search. It extracts and evaluates visual and textual evidence, then produces structured multimodal reports. This connects evidence collection, assessment, and explanation within one workflow, addressing the limitations of approaches that use only text or depend entirely on knowledge already stored in a model.

The authors report that DEFAME surpasses previous methods on VERITE, AVeriTeC, and MOCHEG. They also introduce ClaimReview2024+, whose claims occur after GPT-4o's knowledge cutoff to avoid data leakage from those claims. DEFAME substantially outperforms GPT-4o baselines on this benchmark. These findings support its ability to handle newer claims and indicate potential for real-time fact-checking, while the reported comparisons concern the evaluated benchmarks.
icml-2025-defame-dynamic-evidence-based-.tldr: DEFAME dynamically gathers text and image evidence to verify claims, reporting leading results across several fact-checking benchmarks.

paragraphs: Topic models help identify which themes appear in documents. This paper addresses the central LDA inference problem of determining the topics assigned to each document. It introduces practical algorithms with provable guarantees, using a combinatorial approach that does not rely on gradients to estimate the topic model.

The algorithms approach an optimal posterior probability using only logarithmically many sequential rounds of parallel computation. The claimed exponential improvement concerns this parallel-time measure, also called adaptivity. The approach can additionally guarantee that every learned topic is associated with a known keyword, giving the resulting topics a formal connection to interpretable labels.

The authors also show that their method can preserve independence assumptions required by downstream causal methods that treat topics as interventions. This matters because a useful topic representation must satisfy the assumptions of the analysis that follows it. Across varied text datasets and evaluation settings, the method consistently produces higher semantic quality than the compared LDA algorithms, neural topic models, and language-model-based topic models.
icml-2025-e-lda-toward-interpretable-lda.tldr: E-LDA provides fast parallel topic inference with theoretical guarantees, keyword-based interpretability, and support for downstream causal analysis.

paragraphs: Generative flow methods aim to sample from distributions whose densities need not be normalized. Extending these methods to continuous spaces and imitation learning raises practical difficulties, including losses that are hard to compute and reliance on a separate reward model. This paper introduces Ergodic Generative Flows to address these training obstacles.

The construction uses ergodicity and a finite collection of globally defined, smoothly invertible transformations. The authors establish universality guarantees and obtain a tractable flow-matching loss. Together, these properties connect the ability to represent distributions with a training objective that can actually be evaluated, making the mathematical construction relevant to optimization.

For imitation learning, the paper introduces KL-weakFM, a loss combining cross-entropy with weak flow-matching control. It is designed to learn without a separate reward model. The authors evaluate this approach on two-dimensional toy tasks and NASA datasets defined on the sphere. They also run two-dimensional reinforcement-learning experiments using a specified target reward and the flow-matching loss, demonstrating the framework in both training settings.
icml-2025-ergodic-generative-flows-7e5aa.tldr: Ergodic Generative Flows provide tractable flow-matching training and an imitation-learning objective that needs no separate reward model.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to optimize entire labeled datasets by treating them as distributions of distributions. Each class is represented by the distribution of its features. The dataset is then represented as a mixture whose components are those class-level distributions, preserving the distinction between individual features and the classes they belong to.

The authors equip this nested space with Wasserstein over Wasserstein distance, an optimal-transport-based measure of separation. They then derive the differential structure needed to define gradient flows. These flows describe how a dataset representation can evolve in a direction that decreases a chosen objective, extending gradient-based reasoning to objects that are themselves probability distributions.

To make the framework usable, the paper introduces tractable objectives based on Maximum Mean Discrepancy, with kernels built from Sliced-Wasserstein comparisons between distributions. The authors apply these objectives and flows to transfer learning and dataset distillation. The contribution is a mathematical and computational framework for transforming structured datasets, connecting class-aware representations to a principled notion of improvement.
icml-2025-flowing-datasets-with-wasserst.tldr: The paper models labeled datasets as distributions of class distributions and develops optimal-transport gradient flows for transforming them.

paragraphs: Relationships between brain variables can change with behavioral state, making a single fixed causal graph an incomplete description. This paper develops a method for generating hypotheses about these changing relationships from observed time series. Its motivation is to narrow the set of interventions that neuroscientists need to investigate.

The method represents a dynamic graph as a condition-dependent weighted combination of static graphs. Each component graph can describe nonlinear relationships, so the changing mixture can capture interactions beyond linear patterns. This provides a structured way to express both recurring relationships and changes in their importance as the system's state varies.

In some experiments, the method improves F1 scores for predicted dynamic causal patterns by roughly 22–28% on average over baselines, with some improvements exceeding 60%. A case study using real brain data identifies relationships associated with particular behavioral states. These results support the approach as a tool for proposing state-sensitive causal hypotheses. Its role in the stated neuroscience workflow is to guide subsequent investigation through patterns inferred from observational data.
icml-2025-generating-hypotheses-of-dynam.tldr: A weighted combination of nonlinear static graphs generates hypotheses about changing causal relationships in neural time series.

paragraphs: When benchmark examples enter a model's training data, evaluation can reflect overfitting to those examples. This paper investigates how persistent that effect is. It varies model size, repeated exposure, and training volume, reaching 1.6 billion parameters, 144 presentations per example, and 40 billion training tokens.

The experiments show that small amounts of contamination cause overfitting when model and data sizes follow Chinchilla scaling. However, even 144 exposures can be forgotten when training data exceeds five times that allocation. Continued pretraining of OLMo-7B supports the same pattern. The findings make the amount of subsequent training central to interpreting contamination.

The authors also examine weight decay and find that observed forgetting proceeds faster than cumulative weight decay alone. They use this relationship to estimate forgetting in larger training runs, indicating that several models, including Llama 3 405B, have forgotten data encountered early in training. The result challenges treating any exposure as permanently invalidating an evaluation: the reported effects depend on training scale and when the contaminated examples were seen.
icml-2025-how-much-can-we-forget-about-d.tldr: Experiments show that benchmark contamination can be forgotten with sufficiently extended training, making its impact depend on training scale and exposure timing.

paragraphs: Experimental estimates can vary because different units receive treatment or because different units enter the sample. This paper focuses on the first source, called design uncertainty. That distinction is especially relevant for small fixed samples with heterogeneous treatment effects, including geographical experiments, where standard bootstrap procedures mainly address sampling uncertainty.

Existing causal bootstrap methods account for treatment assignment uncertainty in a narrower setting: completely randomized designs with a difference-in-means estimator. The authors broaden their reach using an integer program that numerically computes a worst-case copula, the dependence structure supplied to the causal bootstrap. This makes the construction usable across a wider range of designs and estimators.

The paper proves asymptotic validity for unconfounded assignments, conditionally unconfounded assignments, and individualistic assignments with bounded confoundedness. It also covers estimators that are linear or quadratic in treatment. Simulations of small geographical experiments demonstrate refined confidence intervals. The contribution connects a computational optimization method to uncertainty assessment while keeping the guarantees tied to the specified assignment classes and estimator forms.
icml-2025-integer-programming-for-genera.tldr: An integer-programming method extends causal bootstrap uncertainty estimates to broader treatment assignments and linear or quadratic treatment estimators.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering organizes data into a tree of progressively finer groups. Similar points should remain together at appropriate levels, allowing the same dataset to be examined at several granularities. The difficulty is that several mathematical objectives for choosing such a tree have strong barriers to efficient approximation.

This paper studies what becomes possible when the algorithm receives auxiliary information from oracles in a learning-augmented framework. The additional information changes the setting in which the clustering problem is solved. The authors develop efficient algorithms for two established objectives, Dasgupta's and Moseley-Wang's, using these oracles to construct approximate hierarchical trees.

The resulting approximation guarantees overcome known hardness barriers in this augmented setting. The role of the oracle is essential to interpreting the claim: the algorithms are given information beyond the ordinary clustering input. The contribution is therefore a demonstration that appropriately structured auxiliary guidance can change what efficient hierarchical clustering can achieve. It connects the quality of a clustering hierarchy to the information available during its construction, across two prominent ways of evaluating such trees.
icml-2025-learning-augmented-hierarchica.tldr: Oracle-provided auxiliary information enables efficient hierarchical clustering approximations that overcome known barriers in the learning-augmented setting.

paragraphs: Data from different modalities often arrives without examples being matched across them. Learning a joint distribution then requires deciding how the separate collections should relate. Minimum Entropy Coupling approaches this by seeking a joint distribution with low entropy while retaining the specified distribution of each modality, known as its marginal.

Existing methods largely handle finite, discrete distributions. This paper introduces DDMEC for continuous data, using generative diffusion models in a cooperative training scheme. The models learn to approximate and reduce joint entropy while satisfying a relaxed form of the marginal constraints. The relaxation is part of the proposed formulation, so the method's matching objective allows flexibility in preserving the individual distributions.

The authors evaluate DDMEC on unsupervised alignment of single-cell multi-omics data and on unpaired image translation. They report that it outperforms specialized methods on these challenging applications. The significance is that one continuous coupling approach can support substantially different kinds of unpaired data, extending the reach of minimum-entropy matching beyond its established discrete setting.
icml-2025-learning-to-match-unpaired-dat.tldr: DDMEC uses cooperating diffusion models to match continuous unpaired data through low joint entropy and relaxed marginal constraints.

paragraphs: Combining diffusion models can sometimes generate results beyond the distributions or sequence lengths addressed by their components. Yet promising examples do not by themselves explain what successful composition means. This paper begins by defining one precise target, called projective composition, so that success can be examined mathematically.

The authors investigate when linear combinations of model scores provably achieve that target. They separately examine whether reverse-diffusion sampling produces the intended combined distribution and identify conditions under which composition fails. Distinguishing the composition rule from the sampling process matters because a proposed combination must also be realized by the procedure that generates samples.

The theory is connected to earlier empirical cases in which composition succeeded or failed without a clear explanation. The paper also proposes a simple heuristic for anticipating the outcome of new combinations. Its contribution is a framework for reasoning about composition, including extrapolation and length generalization, with explicit attention to conditions for success. The predictive heuristic offers practical guidance alongside the conditional theoretical results.
icml-2025-mechanisms-of-projective-compo.tldr: The paper defines projective composition and analyzes when combining diffusion-model scores and sampling can achieve it.

paragraphs: Researchers compare internal neural representations to understand whether artificial or biological systems perform similar computations. This paper asks how closely representation similarity actually tracks functional similarity. It studies the question analytically in two-layer linear networks and supplements that analysis with simulations of nonlinear networks.

The authors find that these two forms of similarity can come apart in either direction. Networks can have similar representations while performing different functions, or similar functions while using different representations. They also show that robustness to input noise and the level of generalization error do not force representations to be specific to the task.

Robustness to parameter noise produces a different result: it restricts representational flexibility and requires task-specific representations in the analysis. This identifies a property of the computation that constrains internal organization beyond functional performance alone. The findings suggest that alignment between representations can reflect computational advantages that functional alignment does not capture. They also sharpen how comparisons of neural codes should be interpreted when drawing conclusions about what networks do.
icml-2025-not-all-solutions-are-created-.tldr: Network representations and functions can vary independently, while robustness to parameter noise constrains representations toward the task.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization problems where one variable is minimized, another is maximized, and a bilinear term couples them. Solving these problems requires both gradient evaluations and matrix-vector multiplications. Earlier optimality results covered particular cases involving strongly convex or affine functions, leaving a broader class of linearly convergent problems unresolved.

The authors establish lower bounds on the computational work needed for this broader class and develop algorithms that match those bounds. The class can include smooth functions without strong convexity. Linear convergence means that the iteration count grows proportionally to the logarithm of inverse target error, giving a precise relationship between additional computation and tighter accuracy.

A central feature of the algorithm is separating the complexities of gradient evaluations and matrix-vector multiplications. This enables it to achieve the optimal count for both kinds of operation simultaneously. The lower bounds also subsume and unify previous results. The advance is a sharper theoretical account of the achievable efficiency for the stated problem class, with optimality measured against explicit computational lower bounds.
icml-2025-on-linear-convergence-in-smoot.tldr: Matching lower bounds and algorithms establish optimal linear convergence for a broader class of bilinearly coupled saddle-point problems.

paragraphs: A verifier can help a language model generate text that satisfies constraints, but the value of this assistance depends on how generation uses it. This paper develops a mathematical framework with a pretrained generator and a process verifier. The verifier determines whether a partial output can still be completed into an acceptable string.

Within this framework, access to verification can make otherwise intractable problems tractable, even in simple settings. The benefits can be information-theoretic or computational. The analysis also shows that tokenwise rejection sampling, which rejects unsuitable token choices during generation, can gain substantially from access to this kind of verifier.

The empirical contribution adds backtracking: the sampler may erase a few recently generated tokens and continue from an earlier point. This modification yields robust improvements in efficiency, accuracy, and diversity over the compared rejection-sampling and nucleus-sampling baselines. The work links theoretical access to useful prefix information with a practical way to revise partial outputs, explaining why verification can help before a complete candidate has been generated.
icml-2025-on-the-query-complexity-of-ver.tldr: Prefix verification can make constrained generation tractable, and allowing tokenwise sampling to backtrack improves empirical efficiency, accuracy, and diversity.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model infer a task from demonstrations included in its input. Empirical work suggests that factual-recall tasks can involve an internal task vector used in vector arithmetic. This paper develops a theoretical explanation based on a hierarchical model of concepts grounded in those observations.

The authors analyze nonlinear residual transformers trained by gradient descent with cross-entropy loss. Their optimization theory explains how these networks can perform factual-recall tasks through vector arithmetic involving retrieved task concepts. This connects the training procedure to an internal mechanism, rather than treating successful in-context learning solely as an observed behavior.

Within the proposed framework, the authors prove convergence of classification error measured by 0–1 loss and establish generalization results that include concept recombination and distribution shifts. Simulations support the theoretical account. These findings help explain advantages of transformers over earlier static embedding approaches. The guarantees apply through the hierarchical concept framework, making the structure of the modeled tasks central to the explanation of learning and generalization.
icml-2025-provable-in-context-vector-ari.tldr: A hierarchical concept framework explains how trained residual transformers can solve factual-recall tasks through in-context vector arithmetic.

paragraphs: Treatment effects can be expressed as an absolute difference in risk or as a ratio between risks. The ratio adds a relative perspective that can make small absolute changes more visible. This paper studies how to estimate risk ratios from observational data, a setting where their theoretical properties have received less attention.

The authors propose several estimators and establish properties including asymptotic normality and associated confidence intervals. They evaluate the estimators using simulated and real-world data, examining bias, efficiency, and robustness across data-generating models. They also assess whether the intervals cover the target value and how long those intervals are.

Because a risk ratio is nonlinear, influence-function analysis yields two distinct efficient estimators with different convergence assumptions. That distinction matters when selecting an estimator: similar efficiency goals can be reached through procedures whose theoretical requirements differ. Combining theory and empirical evidence, the authors recommend one of the two doubly robust estimators. Their recommendation challenges conventional expectations and emphasizes the need to study relative-effect estimation on its own terms.
icml-2025-quantifying-treatment-effects-.tldr: The paper develops and evaluates risk-ratio estimators for observational studies, identifying distinct efficient approaches with different convergence assumptions.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning trajectories are often modeled as having a fixed duration or continuing indefinitely. This paper instead considers random stopping times, including stopping that depends on the trajectory itself. That setting matters when the policy influences both the sequence of events and how long the interaction lasts.

The authors rigorously derive policy-gradient formulas for stochastic and deterministic policies under random time horizons. Since the stopping time typically depends on the policy, its randomness changes the gradient calculation. The work develops complementary views based on complete trajectories and on the state space, and connects the resulting framework to optimal control theory.

Numerical experiments show that the proposed formulas can substantially improve optimization convergence relative to traditional approaches. The finding supports accounting explicitly for policy-dependent duration when computing learning updates. More broadly, the contribution extends the mathematical description of reinforcement learning to interactions whose endpoint is part of the evolving process, supplying gradient formulas that reflect that dependence rather than assuming a predetermined runtime.
icml-2025-reinforcement-learning-with-ra.tldr: New policy-gradient formulas account for random, policy-dependent stopping times and improve optimization convergence in numerical experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies fair clustering when distance information comes from two sources. A strong oracle supplies exact distances at high cost, while a weak oracle supplies cheaper estimates that may be inaccurate. The aim is to obtain a near-optimal fair clustering while making few expensive queries.

The authors construct relative-error coresets for fair k-median clustering. These are compact representations designed to preserve the clustering objective within a factor of one plus a chosen error tolerance. The number of strong-oracle queries is polynomial in the number of clusters, inverse tolerance, and logarithm of the number of input points. This ties expensive information gathering to a much smaller dependence on dataset size.

The results also extend to clustering without fairness constraints, including a broader family of objectives with a constant exponent. Earlier results in this oracle model gave constant-factor approximations exceeding ten for standard clustering, while fair k-median had not been addressed. The contribution therefore improves approximation precision and brings fairness constraints into the same framework for managing inaccurate and costly distance information.
icml-2025-relative-error-fair-clustering.tldr: The paper obtains relative-error fair clustering coresets using few exact-distance queries alongside cheaper inaccurate distance estimates.

paragraphs: Transformer embedding models often need to compress many output vectors into one summary. This paper examines settings where only some input vectors contain information needed for the task and the rest are distractors. The challenge is to preserve the useful information when the proportion of signal and noise changes.

The authors frame pooling as vector quantization with an objective of minimizing signal loss. They show that average pooling, maximum pooling, and class-token summaries can suffer performance collapse as the signal-to-noise ratio varies. An attention-based adaptive pooling method can instead approximate the signal-optimal quantizer within derived error bounds for any signal-to-noise ratio.

The theory is first tested on synthetic supervised data designed to isolate this issue. The evaluation then extends to relational reasoning, multi-agent reinforcement learning, and vision benchmarks with noisy observations, where adaptive pooling provides greater robustness. The work identifies the summarization step as a consequential part of transformer design: retaining relevant information depends on how outputs are combined as well as how those outputs are produced.
icml-2025-robust-noise-attenuation-via-a.tldr: Attention-based adaptive pooling preserves useful transformer information more robustly as the balance between signal and distractors changes.

paragraphs: Accounts of generalization often assume that an overparameterized model reaches a global training-loss minimum. This paper investigates a different possibility in two-layer ReLU networks: increasing the sample count can move training beyond an optimization threshold where interpolation is no longer reached. The resulting solution can nevertheless generalize better.

The analysis centers on an early alignment phase, during which neurons orient toward particular directions. This alignment creates a bias toward simpler solutions. Even with enough parameters to fit the training data, the network may approximate the underlying ground-truth model without attaining the global minimum of training loss.

The authors show that this behavior can produce a drastic reduction in test loss. Their results suggest that the optimization threshold and the associated simplicity bias can be beneficial, linking incomplete fitting to improved generalization in the analyzed setting. The contribution is a theoretical explanation of how the path taken during optimization can favor useful structure, making perfect training fit an insufficient description of why an overparameterized network succeeds.
icml-2025-simplicity-bias-and-optimizati.tldr: Early neuron alignment can steer overparameterized two-layer ReLU networks toward simpler solutions that improve test loss without interpolating training data.

paragraphs: Marginalization sums a function over every assignment to selected inputs. It is generally computationally difficult, but several model classes make it efficient through arithmetic circuits representing multilinear polynomials. This paper asks whether those circuit representations can compactly express every function that admits efficient marginalization.

The authors give a negative answer under the complexity assumption FP differs from #P. They exhibit simple functions whose marginalization is tractable but that lack efficient representations in the known models. To explain the separation, they identify a hierarchy of increasingly strong forms of marginalization, all of which the existing circuit models can compute efficiently.

The paper then provides a complementary completeness result. If an efficient real-RAM algorithm can perform virtual-evidence marginalization for a function, that function's multilinear representation has small arithmetic circuits. These results distinguish ordinary tractable marginalization from stronger computational capabilities. They show why existing representations can fail to capture all efficiently marginalizable functions while also identifying a stronger condition that is sufficient for compact circuit representation.
icml-2025-the-limits-of-tractable-margin.tldr: Under a stated complexity assumption, efficient marginalization does not always imply a compact representation in known arithmetic-circuit models.

paragraphs: Computer agents need to plan actions, interpret screens, and use applications across many steps. Evaluating these abilities is difficult when benchmarks cover only narrow activities or take hours to complete. Windows Agent Arena provides a real Windows environment where agents can use the applications and tools available to human users.

The benchmark includes more than 150 tasks across representative domains. These tasks exercise planning, screen understanding, and tool use within the operating system. Its evaluation infrastructure supports parallel execution, allowing a complete benchmark run in as little as 20 minutes. This reduces the turnaround time for testing changes to multimodal agents.

The evaluations also reveal a substantial capability gap. The best tested agent achieves a 19.5% success rate, compared with 74.5% for humans. These figures describe performance on this Windows benchmark and show how much room remains for improvement in the assessed abilities. The contribution combines a broader setting for practical computer tasks with faster evaluation, making weaknesses easier to measure during agent development.
icml-2025-windows-agent-arena-evaluating.tldr: Windows Agent Arena enables fast evaluation on over 150 real Windows tasks and reveals a large success-rate gap between tested agents and humans.
